note: Short for 'you have come to family and (trodden) easy ground'. The reply is 'ahlan bik'. Both words end in the accusative -an, written with two fatḥa marks over an alif.
The set reply is 'ṣabāḥ an-nūr' (morning of light). 'Ṣabāḥ' and 'khayr' form an iḍāfa (possessive chain): only the second word takes al-.
Reply: 'masāʾ an-nūr'. Used from the afternoon onwards. The final hamza of 'masāʾ' sits on the line after a long ā.
Colloquial: 'kīfak / kīfik' (Levant), 'izzayyak / izzayyik' (Egypt). The Arabic question mark ؟ is mirrored.
The usual answer to 'kayfa l-ḥāl', often followed by 'al-ḥamdu li-llāh'. 'Khayr' (good) is the same word as in 'ṣabāḥ al-khayr'.
Said after eating, on good news, or simply as 'fine, thanks'. Root ḥ-m-d (praise) also gives the names Muḥammad, Aḥmad and Ḥamīd.
From ʿafw (pardon, forgiveness). Doubles as a reply to 'shukran' and as 'excuse me' when interrupting. Another frozen accusative like 'shukran'.
An active participle, so it agrees with the speaker: a woman says 'āsifa'. The alif with madda (آ) marks hamza + long ā at the start.
Colloquial: 'aywa' (Egypt), 'ē' (Levant). 'Balā' is used to answer 'yes' to a negative question, like French 'si'.
Also negates present-tense verbs: 'lā aʿrif' (I don't know). The ligature lām-alif لا is written as one shape.
A form V verb from the root sh-r-f (honour). The 'we' is polite, like saying 'it's an honour'.
The suffix -ka (to a man) or -ki (to a woman) is only shown by a vowel mark. 'Ism' (name) begins with a connecting hamza, so it is written without the hamza sign.
The suffix -ī means 'my'. No verb 'to be' is needed in the present: 'ismī Layla' = 'my name (is) Layla'.

literal: may you wake up in good(ness)
note: Reply: 'wa anta min ahlihi' (and you are of its people). To a woman: 'tuṣbiḥīn ʿalā khayr'.
'Liqāʾ' (meeting) is from l-q-y, 'to meet'. Slightly more formal than 'maʿa s-salāma'; often what you hear at the end of broadcasts.
'Anta' (you, m.) and 'anti' (you, f.) are spelled the same without vowel marks; context or the final vowel decides.
The everyday way to call a waiter or ask a stranger. Root s-m-ḥ (permit, be tolerant), also behind 'samāḥa' (tolerance).
Root b-r-k (blessing), also in 'baraka'. The usual reply is 'Allāh yubārik fīk' (God bless you).

en: Enjoy your meal / to your health
note: Said to someone eating or after a job well done; the reply is 'Allāh yaʿāfīk'. In the Maghreb 'ʿāfiya' can mean 'fire', so there people say 'bi-ṣ-ṣaḥḥa' instead.
'Jazīl' means abundant. Both words carry the -an ending, so the adjective agrees with the noun in case.
A polite reply to thanks: helping you was my duty. 'Wājib' (duty) is also the word for 'homework' in schools.
'Sayyid' and 'sayyida' are used before names like Mr./Mrs. The Spanish title 'Cid' (El Cid) comes from this word.

en: Please, go ahead / here you are
note: Said when handing something over, offering a seat, or letting someone pass. Same root f-ḍ-l as 'min faḍlik'. To a woman: 'tafaḍḍalī'.
Said in admiration of a child, a house, an achievement, traditionally to ward off envy. Compare 'in shāʾ Allāh' (if God wills) for the future.
'Nahār' is daytime as opposed to night ('layl'). 'Saʿīd' (happy) is also a common man's name.
Source of English 'cipher' and, via Italian 'zefiro', 'zero'. Eastern Arabic numerals: ٠١٢٣٤٥٦٧٨٩, written left to right even inside right-to-left text.
Follows the noun like an adjective and agrees in gender: 'kitāb wāḥid' (one book), 'bint wāḥida' (one girl). Numeral ١.
Rarely needed with nouns: Arabic has a dual ending -ān/-ayn ('kitābān' = two books). Feminine 'ithnatān'. Numeral ٢. Colloquial: 'itnēn / tnēn'.
Numbers 3-10 show reverse agreement: the form with tāʾ marbūṭa (thalātha) goes with masculine nouns, 'thalāth' with feminine ones. The noun follows in the plural. Numeral ٣.
Root r-b-ʿ, also in 'arbiʿāʾ' (Wednesday, the fourth day) and 'rubʿ' (quarter). Numeral ٤.
Related to 'khamīs' (Thursday, the fifth day) and the 'khamsa' hand amulet. Numeral ٥, written like a small circle in some styles.
Numeral ٦, which looks like a Latin 7. The original root s-d-s survives in 'sādis' (sixth).
Numeral ٧ is a V shape. 'Usbūʿ' (week, 'seven-day thing') shares the root s-b-ʿ.
Numeral ٨, an upside-down V. Note the initial ث (th as in 'thin'), often pronounced t or s in colloquial speech.
Numeral ٩. Easily confused by ear with 'sabʿa' (seven) and 'sitta' (six); listen for the first consonant.
Numeral ١٠. The -ūn/-īn ending turns it into 'ʿishrūn' (twenty). Root ʿ-sh-r also gives 'ʿāshūrāʾ' (the 10th of Muḥarram).
11-19 are compounds 'unit + ʿashar'. The counted noun follows in the singular accusative: 'aḥada ʿashara kitāban'.
Built on the dual of 'ithnān'. A dozen is 'dasta' (from Persian) in everyday speech.
Tens take the sound masculine plural ending -ūn (-īn after prepositions and in speech: 'ʿishrīn'). 21 = 'wāḥid wa-ʿishrūn', 'one and twenty'.
'Thalāth' + -ūn. 40 'arbaʿūn', 60 'sittūn', 70 'sabʿūn', 80 'thamānūn', 90 'tisʿūn' follow the same pattern.
'Khams' + -ūn. Colloquial 'khamsīn' also names the hot spring wind of Egypt, said to blow for fifty days.
Also spelled مائة with a silent alif, a very old spelling convention. 200 is the dual 'miʾatān'; 300 'thalāthumiʾa'.
Plural 'ālāf': 'thalāthat ālāf' = 3,000. 'Alf layla wa-layla' is the Arabic title of the Thousand and One Nights.
A European loanword, plural 'malāyīn'. 'Milyār' is a billion (as in French).
Feminine 'ūlā', as in 'al-marra l-ūlā' (the first time). Ordinals 2nd-10th use the fāʿil pattern: thānī, thālith, rābiʿ, khāmis...
Feminine 'thāniya', which is also the noun 'second' (unit of time). Root th-n-y, 'to fold, double'.
Plural 'anṣāf'. 'As-sāʿa l-wāḥida wa-n-niṣf' = half past one. Colloquial 'nuṣṣ'.
From the root of 'arbaʿa' (four). 'Ar-Rubʿ al-Khālī', the Empty Quarter, is the great desert of Arabia.
'Marra wāḥida' = once, 'marratayn' = twice (dual), 'thalāth marrāt' = three times. 'Marra ukhrā' = again.
Plural 'arqām'. 'Raqm al-hātif' = phone number. 'ʿAdad' is the word for a quantity or a count.
Plural 'ummahāt'. Parents are often addressed by their eldest son's name: 'Umm Aḥmad'. 'Ummī' = my mother. Colloquial also 'māma'.
'Abī' = my father; 'Abū' appears in names ('Abū Bakr', father of Bakr). Plural 'ābāʾ'. Colloquial 'bāba'.
Plural 'ikhwa' (brothers) or 'ikhwān' (brethren). 'Akhī' (my brother) is a common friendly address to any man.
Plural 'akhawāt'. The final -t is part of the root here, not a tāʾ marbūṭa.
Plural 'abnāʾ'. In names it is written 'bin' between two names: 'ʿAlī bin Abī Ṭālib'. Begins with a connecting hamza.
Plural 'banāt'. Also 'girl' in general. 'Ibna' is the more formal word for daughter.

example.en: I have a daughter and a son.

note: Plural 'ajdād' (ancestors). Colloquial: 'sīdī' and 'sittī' (Levant), 'gidd' and 'tēta' (Egypt). Not the same as 'jiddan' (very).
Father's brother or sister. Plural 'aʿmām'. 'Yā ʿammī' is a respectful way to address an older man.
Mother's brother or sister; Arabic always distinguishes the two sides of the family. Plural 'akhwāl'.
Arabic has no single word for cousin: 'ibn/bint ʿamm' (father's side), 'ibn/bint khāl' (mother's side).
The same word as 'pair'. 'Zawjī' = my husband, 'zawjatī' = my wife. Colloquial also 'jōz / gōz' and 'marti' (my wife).
Plural 'ʿāʾilāt'. 'Usra' is the nuclear family, 'ahl' one's people or relatives, as in 'ahlan'.
Plural 'aṭfāl', a broken plural on the pattern afʿāl. 'Ṭifla' = a little girl.
Plural 'rijāl'. Colloquial 'rājil / rijjāl'. Beware 'rijl' with the same letters: 'foot, leg'.
The plural 'nisāʾ' comes from a different root entirely. With al- the spelling changes to 'al-marʾa'. Colloquial 'mara' can sound rude; 'sayyida' is safer.
Plural 'aṣdiqāʾ'. From ṣ-d-q (truth, sincerity): a friend is one who is true. 'Ṣāḥib' is the usual colloquial word.
Plural 'awlād', which in colloquial speech means 'children' in general. Root w-l-d, 'to give birth', also in 'mawlid' (birthday).
Plural 'shabāb', which also means 'youth' collectively and is a common football-club name (ash-Shabāb).
The more formal word for father; 'wālida' = mother. 'Al-wālidān' (dual) = the parents.
Plural 'nās' (people) is from the same root. 'Ḥuqūq al-insān' = human rights.
A collective noun with no singular of its own; 'shakhṣ' (person, pl. ashkhāṣ) fills the gap. Sūrat an-Nās is the last chapter of the Qurʾan.
Plural 'jīrān'. A hadith famously stresses the rights of the neighbour; 'jāra' is the feminine.
Plural 'aḥfād'. The pattern faʿīl is common for people and qualities (ṣadīq, kabīr, jadīd).
Plural of 'qarīb', which as an adjective means 'near, close'. Root q-r-b, as in 'qurb' (nearness).
From r-ḍ-ʿ, 'to nurse'. Everyday speech also uses 'bēbī' or 'ṭifl ṣaghīr' (small child).
Flat 'khubz ʿarabī' is the everyday bread. In Egypt bread is called 'ʿēsh', literally 'life'.
Plural 'miyāh' (waters, as in 'water supply'). Colloquial 'mayya' (Egypt), 'mayy' (Levant). The final hamza sits alone on the line.
From ḥ-l-b, 'to milk'. In Egypt milk is 'laban', which in the Levant means yoghurt instead: a classic regional trap.
Source of 'coffee' via Turkish 'kahve' and Italian 'caffè'. 'Qahwa ʿarabiyya' is lightly roasted and spiced with cardamom.
From Chinese 'chá' via Persian, like Russian 'chai'. Usually served sweet, often with mint ('shāy bi-n-naʿnāʿ').
English 'sugar' comes from this word via medieval Latin and Old French; it reached Arabic from Persian and ultimately Sanskrit 'śarkarā'.
'Mālīḥ' = salty. 'Al-Baḥr al-Mālīḥ' is a nickname for the sea, and 'ʿaysh wa-milḥ' (bread and salt) means a bond of hospitality.
Plural 'luḥūm'. 'Laḥm ghanam' = mutton, 'laḥm baqar' = beef. The city name Bethlehem ('Bayt Laḥm') looks like 'house of meat' in Arabic.
A collective noun; one chicken is 'dajāja'. Colloquial Egyptian 'firākh', Levantine 'jāj'.
Collective; 'samaka' is one fish, plural 'asmāk'. Many food words work this way: tuffāḥ (apples), tuffāḥa (an apple).
Also spelled 'ruzz'. Arabic 'aruzz' and English 'rice' both go back to Greek 'oryza'.
Collective; one egg is 'bayḍa'. From the same root as 'abyaḍ' (white).
Also 'jubna'. 'Jubn abyaḍ' is the white brined cheese eaten at breakfast across the region. Colloquial Egyptian 'gibna'.
Plural 'fawākih'. A fruit seller is a 'fākihānī'.
Literally 'greens', from kh-ḍ-r (green), the root of 'akhḍar'. Also 'khuḍrawāt' in formal writing.
Collective; 'tuffāḥa' is one apple. 'ʿAṣīr tuffāḥ' = apple juice.
Named after Portugal, whose traders brought the sweet orange east; the same word names the colour. One orange is 'burtuqāla'.
'Zayt zaytūn' = olive oil. 'Zayt' and 'zaytūn' (olives) share the root; Spanish 'aceite' (oil) is borrowed from 'az-zayt'.
Collective; one olive is 'zaytūna'. Jabal az-Zaytūn is the Mount of Olives in Jerusalem. Spanish 'aceituna' comes from this word.
From ʿ-ṣ-r, 'to squeeze, press'. 'ʿAṣīr burtuqāl' = orange juice. 'ʿAṣr' (afternoon) is the same root.
Collective; 'tamra' is one date. Dried dates; fresh ones are 'balaḥ' or 'ruṭab'. Traditionally the first food eaten at iftar.
'Shahr al-ʿasal' is the honeymoon, a calque that also exists in English and French. 'ʿAsal' is also a term of endearment.
The dish is really 'ḥummuṣ bi-ṭaḥīna' (chickpeas with sesame paste); 'ḥummuṣ' alone just means chickpeas.
In Egypt the same fried patties, made from fava beans rather than chickpeas, are called 'ṭaʿmiyya'.
Also used figuratively: 'zubdat al-kalām' = the gist (literally 'the butter of the talk').
Plural 'maṭāʿim'. The prefix ma- makes place nouns from roots: ṭ-ʿ-m (food) gives 'maṭʿam', as k-t-b gives 'maktab' (office).
Plural 'maqāhī'. From 'qahwa'; in Egypt the traditional café is simply called 'qahwa' as well.
'Qāʾima' = list. Many places simply use the loanword 'menyū'. 'Ṭaʿām' = food, from the same root as 'maṭʿam'.
Formal word; in practice people call a waiter with 'law samaḥt' or (Egypt) 'yā usṭā'. The French loan 'garsōn' is also widely heard.
A loan from Italian 'tavola'. Colloquial Levantine 'ṭāwle', also the name of the backgammon game played on café tables.
From f-ṭ-r. 'Ifṭār' is the same root and names the evening meal that breaks the Ramadan fast; 'ʿĪd al-Fiṭr' ends the month.
Traditionally the main meal of the day. Do not confuse with 'ghadan' (tomorrow), spelled with the same first letters.
Same root as 'ʿishāʾ', the night prayer. Verb: 'taʿashshā' (to have dinner).
'Ḥisāb' (reckoning, account) is from ḥ-s-b, 'to count'; it is also the word for a bank account and for arithmetic.
'Ṭalab' = an order or a request; 'ṭālib' (student) is literally 'one who seeks' (knowledge).
Present tense of 'arāda'. Colloquial: 'biddī' (Levant), 'ʿāyiz / ʿāyza' (Egypt), 'abghā' (Gulf).
Plural 'akwāb'. A small coffee cup is a 'finjān', a word that also passed into Turkish and Greek.
'Zujāj' is glass as a material. Colloquial Egyptian 'izāza', Levantine 'qannīne'.
Plural 'ṣuḥūn'. Also 'ṭabaq' (pl. aṭbāq), which doubles as 'dish' in the sense of a prepared food.
Plural 'malāʿiq'. From l-ʿ-q (to lick); the mi- prefix marks a tool, as in 'miftāḥ' (key).
Originally 'thorn, spike'; the eating fork took its name from the shape. Plural 'shuwak'.
Plural 'sakākīn'. Can be masculine or feminine in classical usage.
From l-dh-dh (pleasure). Note the two ذ letters, pronounced like 'th' in 'this'. Colloquial also 'ṭayyib' and 'zākī'.
From 'jūʿ' (hunger). Colloquial 'jūʿān / gaʿān'. The hamza sits on a yāʾ-shaped seat in the middle of the word.
From 'ʿaṭash' (thirst). Feminine 'ʿaṭshā' in classical grammar, 'ʿaṭshāna' in speech. The pattern faʿlān marks states (taʿbān, jawʿān).
From 'ḥulw' (sweet). Baklava, kunāfa and basbūsa are typical. The singular 'ḥalwā' gave English 'halva'.
From Persian 'shūrbā' via Turkish 'çorba'; the classical word 'ḥasāʾ' is rarely heard. 'Shūrbat ʿadas' (lentil soup) is a staple.
A European loan (Italian 'insalata'). 'Salaṭa ʿarabiyya' is chopped tomato, cucumber and parsley.
Passive participle of 'shariba'. Plural 'mashrūbāt'; 'mashrūbāt sākhina' = hot drinks. 'Sharāb' is syrup or, classically, wine.
The verbal noun of 'ḥajaza' (to reserve, to book). 'ʿIndī ḥajz' = I have a reservation. Also used for hotels and flights.

example.en: I have a reservation under the name Ahmad.

note: Spelled the same as 'dhahab' (gold); only the vowels differ. Colloquial speech prefers 'rāḥ' (Levant/Egypt).
Root w-ṣ-l (connect, reach): 'wuṣūl' = arrival, 'ittiṣāl' = phone call, 'waṣl' = receipt.
A form III verb (fāʿala pattern). 'Safar' = travel, journey; 'musāfir' = traveller; English 'safari' came through Swahili from this root.
'Suʾāl' = question (pl. asʾila), 'masʾūl' = responsible (literally 'asked'). The hamza sits on an alif in the middle.
Colloquial 'wēn' (Levant/Gulf), 'fēn' (Egypt). 'Min ayna' = from where; 'ilā ayna' = to where.
'ʿAlā l-yamīn' = on the right. 'Al-Yaman' (Yemen) is traditionally the land 'to the right' of Mecca when facing east.
'ʿAlā l-yasār' = on the left. Colloquial often 'shimāl', which also means 'north'.

example.en: The bank is on the left.

note: Colloquial but universally understood; in Egypt it also means 'immediately, always'. Formal: 'ilā l-amām' (forwards).
'Qarīb min' = near to. As a noun, 'relative' (pl. aqārib). 'Qarīban' = soon.
'Baʿīd ʿan' = far from. 'Abʿad' = further; 'buʿd' = distance, dimension.
'Hunāka' = there. Colloquial 'hōn' (Levant), 'hina' (Egypt).
Also used for 'there is / there are': 'hunāka mushkila' = there is a problem.
Plural 'kharāʾiṭ'. Borrowed from Greek 'chartēs' (the same source as English 'chart').
From ṭ-y-r (fly): 'ṭāʾira' = aeroplane, 'ṭayr' = bird, 'ṭayyār' = pilot. Plural 'maṭārāt'.
Plural 'fanādiq'. From Greek 'pandocheion' (inn); the Italian 'fondaco' (trading warehouse) came back from Arabic.

example.en: The hotel is near the sea.

note: 'Jawāz' = permit, from j-w-z (to pass, be allowed). Often shortened to 'jawāz'.
Plural 'tadhākir'. From dh-k-r (remember, mention). Colloquial 'tazkara'.

example.en: a return ticket (going and coming back)

note: Plural 'riḥlāt'. Also 'flight'. The famous travelogue of Ibn Baṭṭūṭa is simply called 'ar-Riḥla'. 'Riḥla saʿīda!' = bon voyage.
Plural 'ḥaqāʾib'. Colloquial 'shanṭa' (from Turkish 'çanta'), the word most travellers actually hear.
Plural 'shawāriʿ'. Street signs: 'shāriʿ' + name, e.g. 'Shāriʿ al-Ḥamrā' in Beirut.
'Janūb' = south, 'sharq' = east, 'gharb' = west. 'Al-Maghrib' (Morocco) is literally 'the west', where the sun sets.
'Janūbī' = southern. 'Janūb as-Sūdān' = South Sudan.
Plural 'jihāt'. 'Min jiha ... wa-min jiha ukhrā' = on the one hand ... on the other. 'Ittijāh' is direction of movement.
A woman says 'anā ḍāʾiʿa'. From ḍ-y-ʿ (be lost, wasted). Colloquial: 'anā tāyih / tāyha'.
Plural 'suyyāḥ' or 'sāʾiḥūn'. 'Siyāḥa' = tourism. Root s-y-ḥ, to roam.
Coined from s-y-r (to move, travel) when cars arrived; classically it meant a caravan. Colloquial Egyptian 'ʿarabiyya'. Plural 'sayyārāt'.
The official word; everyone says 'bāṣ' or 'utūbīs' (from French 'autobus'). Plural 'ḥāfilāt'.
Plural 'qiṭārāt' or 'quṭur'. Classically a string of camels in a line, from q-ṭ-r (to line up).
Active participle of 'ṭāra' (to fly), from the root ṭ-y-r, like 'maṭār' (airport). Plural 'ṭāʾirāt'.
A loanword; the Arabic coinage 'sayyārat ujra' (hire car) appears on signs. In Egypt shared taxis are 'mīkrobāṣ', in the Levant 'sarvīs'.

example.en: I want a taxi to the airport.

note: From d-r-j (to roll, step). 'Darrāja nāriyya' (fire bicycle) = motorbike. Colloquial Egyptian 'ʿagala' (wheel).
Plural 'sufun'. A small boat is 'qārib' or 'markab'. English 'admiral' comes from 'amīr al-baḥr' (commander of the sea).
From ḥ-ṭ-ṭ (to put down, alight). Used for train, bus and metro stations and for petrol stations ('maḥaṭṭat banzīn').
Cairo's metro (1987) was the first in Africa and the Arab world; Dubai, Riyadh, Algiers and Doha followed.
Used for cars, buses and horses alike. 'Rākib' = passenger (pl. rukkāb), 'markab' = boat.
A form VIII verb (iftaʿala). 'Intiẓār' = waiting; 'ghurfat al-intiẓār' = waiting room. Colloquial: 'istannā'.

example.en: I waited an hour for the bus.

note: A hollow verb: the middle letter changes (qāda / qudtu). 'Qāʾid' = leader, driver; 'qiyāda' = driving, leadership. Colloquial: 'sāq'.
Active participle of 'sāqa' (to drive). Colloquial Egyptian 'sawwāq', Levantine 'shōfēr' (from French).
Plural 'ṭuruq'. 'Ṭarīqa' = method, way of doing, and also a Sufi order. 'Fī ṭ-ṭarīq' = on the way.
From m-r-r (to pass). 'Shurṭat al-murūr' = traffic police. Colloquial Egyptian 'zaḥma' means a traffic jam or any crowd.
From w-q-f (to stand, stop). 'Mawqif al-bāṣ' = bus stop; 'mawqif sayyārāt' = car park. Also 'stance, position'.
From 'benzine'. 'Maḥaṭṭat banzīn' = petrol station. Diesel is 'dīzil' or 'māzūt'.
'Bi-surʿa' = quickly; 'surʿa' = speed. 'Qiṭār sarīʿ' = express train.
'Bi-buṭʾ' = slowly. Colloquial: 'shway shway' (little by little) is the usual way to say 'slowly!'.
'Qif' is the imperative of 'waqafa'; it is the word on Arabic stop signs. Colloquial: 'hina kwayyis' (Egypt: here is fine).
'Ujra' = fare, wage, rent, from ʾ-j-r. Agree the price before getting into a taxi without a meter ('ʿaddād').
Plural 'jusūr'. In Egypt a bridge or flyover is a 'kubrī' (from Turkish 'köprü').
Plural 'mawāniʾ'. Borrowed in antiquity from Greek 'limēn'. Mīnā is also a woman's name.
'Jaww' = air, atmosphere, and also 'weather' or 'mood'. Usually just 'riḥla' at the airport; 'raqm ar-riḥla' = flight number.
Also 'haste' (ʿajala = hurry). In Egypt 'ʿagala' is the normal word for bicycle.
'Yawm' = day (pl. ayyām); with al- it means 'today'. 'Yawm al-...' names the days of the week.
Colloquial: 'bukra' (Egypt/Levant), 'bāchir' (Gulf). Another frozen accusative in -an.
Also 'al-bāriḥa' (the past night), which is the usual colloquial word: 'imbāriḥ' (Egypt), 'mbāriḥ' (Levant).
Colloquial: 'dilwaʾti' (Egypt), 'hallaʾ' (Levant), 'al-ḥīn' (Gulf). The madda on آ marks hamza + long ā.
Plural 'sāʿāt'. 'Kam as-sāʿa?' = what time is it? 'As-sāʿa l-khāmisa' = five o'clock (literally 'the fifth hour').
Plural 'daqāʾiq'. The adjective 'daqīq' means precise or fine; 'daqīq' as a noun is flour.
Plural 'asābīʿ'. From 'sabʿa' (seven). 'Nihāyat al-usbūʿ' = weekend, which in most Arab countries is Friday-Saturday.
Plural 'shuhūr' or 'ashhur'. The Islamic (hijrī) months are lunar; Levantine Arabic uses old Semitic month names, Egypt uses European ones.
Plural 'sanawāt' or 'sinūn'. 'ʿĀm' is a synonym: 'kull ʿām wa-antum bi-khayr' is the all-purpose festive greeting.
Days 1-5 are numbered from Sunday: al-aḥad, al-ithnayn, ath-thulāthāʾ, al-arbiʿāʾ, al-khamīs. 'Yawm' may precede each.
From 'ithnān' (two). Colloquial 'il-itnēn / it-tanēn'.
ث is a sun letter, so al- is pronounced 'ath-'. Colloquial 'it-talāt'.
From 'arbaʿa' (four). Colloquial 'il-arbaʿ'.
From 'khamsa' (five). Thursday evening starts the weekend in much of the region.
From j-m-ʿ (gather), for the congregational noon prayer. The usual day off; 'jāmiʿ' (mosque) and 'jāmiʿa' (university) share the root.
Cognate with Hebrew 'shabbat'. س is a sun letter: 'as-sabt'.
'Ṣabāḥan' = in the morning (as in '9 ṣabāḥan', 9 a.m.). 'Ṣubḥ' is dawn and the dawn prayer.
'Layla' = one night (and a woman's name); plural 'layālī'. 'Alf layla wa-layla' = the Thousand and One Nights.
'Ẓuhr' = noon and the noon prayer; 'ʿaṣr' = late afternoon. ظ is a sun letter, hence 'aẓ-ẓuhr'.
From b-k-r (early morning), the root of 'bukra' (tomorrow) and the name Bakr. Colloquial 'badrī' (Egypt), 'bakkīr' (Levant).
'Taʾakhkhara' = to be late. 'Ākhir' = last, 'al-ākhira' = the hereafter. Agrees with the person: 'mutaʾakhkhira' for a woman.
From d-w-m (to last). 'Dāʾim' = permanent. Colloquial 'dayman' or 'ʿalā ṭūl' (Egypt).
Plural of 'ḥīn' (a time, a moment) with the adverbial -an. 'Ḥīna' = when (conjunction).
The ninth lunar month, of fasting. Greeting: 'Ramaḍān karīm' (generous Ramadan). From r-m-ḍ, scorching heat.
'Bidāya' = beginning; 'mubtadiʾ' = beginner. The final hamza makes 'badaʾtu' (I began).
Plural 'alwān'. Basic colours use the pattern afʿal (m.) / faʿlāʾ (f.): aḥmar / ḥamrāʾ.
'Al-Baḥr al-Aḥmar' = the Red Sea. 'Al-Ḥamrāʾ' (the Alhambra in Granada) is the feminine: 'the red one'. Plural 'ḥumr'.
Feminine 'zarqāʾ', as in the Jordanian city az-Zarqāʾ. Plural 'zurq'.
Root kh-ḍ-r also gives 'khuḍār' (vegetables). The hero al-Khiḍr, 'the green one', is a figure of Islamic legend.
'Ṣufr' is also the word for brass. 'Ṣafrāʾ' is the feminine and the word for bile.
Feminine 'sawdāʾ'. 'As-Sūdān' means 'the (land of the) blacks'. 'Al-Ḥajar al-Aswad' is the Black Stone of the Kaaba.
Feminine 'bayḍāʾ'; 'ad-Dār al-Bayḍāʾ' (the white house) is Casablanca. Same root as 'bayḍ' (eggs).
From 'bunn' (coffee beans) + the adjectival ending -ī (nisba). 'Asmar' is used for brown skin or hair.
From 'ramād' (ashes) + -ī. Secondary colours are mostly nisba adjectives of this kind.
'Burtuqāl' (oranges) + -ī, so the colour is named after the fruit, which is named after Portugal.
From 'ward' (roses, pl. wurūd), itself an old Persian loan. 'Māʾ ward' = rose water.
From 'banafsaj' (violet, the flower), a Persian loan. 'Urjuwānī' is the older word for purple, from the Phoenician dye.
From 'dhahab' (gold). 'Al-ʿaṣr adh-dhahabī' = the golden age.
'Azraq fātiḥ' = light blue. From f-t-ḥ (to open); 'al-Fātiḥa' is the opening chapter of the Qurʾan.
'Akhḍar ghāmiq' = dark green. Colloquial also 'ghāmiʾ'. For darkness of night use 'muẓlim'.
Plural 'ashkāl'. Also 'appearance' and 'kind': 'shaklak taʿbān' = you look tired. 'Tashkīl' = the vowel marks on Arabic letters.
Plural 'dawāʾir'. Also 'department, district'. Root d-w-r (turn), as in 'dawr' (role, turn) and 'dawra' (course).
From 'arbaʿa' (four). 'Mitr murabbaʿ' = square metre. A public square is a 'maydān' or 'sāḥa'.
From 'thalātha' (three). 'Muthallath Barmūdā' = the Bermuda triangle.
Plural 'khuṭūṭ'. Also 'handwriting, calligraphy' ('al-khaṭṭ al-ʿarabī') and 'phone line'. 'Khaṭṭāṭ' = calligrapher.
Plural 'nuqaṭ' or 'niqāṭ'. The dots on letters (ب ت ث) are 'nuqaṭ'; also 'point' in a score and 'drop' of liquid.
'Najm' (collective) / 'najma' (one star, also 'a star' as in celebrity), plural 'nujūm'. 'ʿIlm an-nujūm' is astrology.
From the same root d-w-r as 'dāʾira'. 'Ṭāwila mustadīra' = a round table.
Plural 'kibār'; 'akbar' = bigger / greatest, as in 'Allāhu akbar'. Also 'old' of people.
Plural 'ṣighār'; 'aṣghar' = smaller / smallest. Also 'young'. Colloquial Egyptian 'ṣughayyar'.
Plural 'ruʾūs'. Also 'cape, headland' (Raʾs al-Khayma) and 'capital' in 'raʾs māl'. 'Raʾīs' (president, boss) is the same root.
Also 'spring (of water)' and the name of the letter ع. Dual 'ʿaynān', plural 'ʿuyūn'. 'Yā ʿaynī' is a term of endearment.
Grammatically feminine, like most paired body parts. Dual 'yadān', plural 'aydī'. 'Yad bi-yad' = hand in hand.
Feminine; dual 'qadamān', plural 'aqdām'. 'Kurat al-qadam' = football. 'Mashyan ʿalā l-aqdām' = on foot. Also 'foot' as a unit of length.
Plural 'qulūb'. From q-l-b (to turn over): 'inqilāb' = coup, 'qalaba' = to flip. 'Min kull qalbī' = with all my heart.
Plural 'buṭūn'. 'Raqṣ baladī' is what Arabs call what English calls belly dance. 'Bāṭin' = inner, hidden.
One of the few two-letter nouns; in a possessive chain it becomes 'fū': 'fūhu' = his mouth. Colloquial 'tumm' (Levant), 'buʾʾ' (Egypt).
Plural 'unūf'. Colloquial 'manākhīr' (Egypt), 'mnukhār' (Levant). 'Anfa' = pride, as in 'holding one's nose high'.
Dual 'udhunān', plural 'ādhān'. 'Adhān' (call to prayer) and 'muʾadhdhin' come from the same root: to announce, to make hear.
Plural 'asnān'. Also 'age': 'kam sinnuk?' = how old are you? 'Ṭabīb asnān' = dentist.
Spelled the same as 'shiʿr' (poetry); only the vowel differs. One hair is 'shaʿra'.
Same letters as 'ẓuhr' (noon). 'ʿan ẓahr qalb' = by heart. Plural 'ẓuhūr'.
Plural 'dimāʾ'. 'Faṣīlat ad-dam' = blood type. 'Khafīf ad-dam' (light of blood) = funny, charming.
Plural 'aṭibbāʾ'. 'Ṭibb' = medicine (the science). The loanword 'duktūr' is just as common in speech.
From sh-f-y (heal): 'shifāʾ' = recovery, as in the wish 'shifāʾ ʿājil' (speedy recovery). Plural 'mustashfayāt'.
'Ṣaydalī' = pharmacist. Marked by a green cross or crescent; many sell medicine without a prescription.
Plural 'adwiya'. The root d-w-y also gives 'dāʾ' (disease) and 'dāwā' (to treat).
Plural 'marḍā'. 'Maraḍ' = illness. As a noun, 'patient'. Colloquial also 'taʿbān' (tired, unwell).
Plural 'ālām'. 'ʿIndī alam fī...' = I have a pain in... 'Muʾlim' = painful. Do not confuse with 'ʿalam' (flag).
From ṣ-d-ʿ (to split). 'ʿIndī ṣudāʿ' = I have a headache. Colloquial also 'rāsī byūjaʿnī' (my head hurts).
'Ṣiḥḥa' = health; 'ṣiḥḥī' = healthy. 'Ṣaḥḥa!' is said to someone who sneezes or finishes a meal. 'Ṣaḥīḥ' = correct.
Hollow verb: 'nāma' but 'nimtu' (I slept). 'Nawm' = sleep; 'ghurfat an-nawm' = bedroom. 'Tuṣbiḥ ʿalā khayr' is what you say before it.
A form IV doubled verb: 'aḥassa' but 'aḥsastu' (I felt). 'Aḥassa bi-' = to feel something; 'iḥsās' = feeling, sensation. Also 'shaʿara bi-'.
'Taʿab' = fatigue. The faʿlān pattern marks temporary states. Colloquially also 'unwell'. Formal: 'mutʿab'.
Plural 'ajsām'. 'Jasad' is the body as flesh; 'jism' is also 'object' in physics.
Plural 'buyūt'. Also a line of poetry. 'Bayt' is cognate with Hebrew 'beth', the letter name that gave Greek 'beta'. Colloquial 'bēt'.
Plural 'ghuraf'. 'Ghurfat an-nawm' = bedroom. Colloquial Egyptian 'ōḍa' (from Turkish 'oda').
From ṭ-b-kh (cook), with the ma- place prefix. Plural 'maṭābikh'.
Also 'bath-house' (the Turkish bath). From ḥ-m-m (heat). With a single m, 'ḥamām' means 'pigeons'.
Plural 'abwāb'. Also 'chapter' and 'gate', as in 'Bāb al-Mandab'. Appears in many city gate names.
From n-f-dh (to pass through). Plural 'nawāfidh'. Colloquial 'shubbāk' (Levant/Egypt), also used for a ticket window.
Plural 'asirra'. 'Ghurfa bi-sarīrayn' = a room with two beds (dual). Classically also 'throne'.
Plural 'karāsī'. 'Āyat al-Kursī' (the Throne Verse) is a famous Qurʾanic verse. Also 'seat' in parliament.
From f-t-ḥ (open), with the mi- tool prefix. Plural 'mafātīḥ'.
Light as brightness; 'ḍawʾ' is light as a physical ray. Common name (Nūr, Nūra). 'Miṣbāḥ' or colloquial 'lamba' = lamp.
Plural 'ḥīṭān'. 'Ḥāʾiṭ al-Burāq' is the Arabic name of the Western Wall. Also 'jidār' (pl. judrān).
Also 'earth, land', feminine. Plural 'arāḍī' (lands, territories). 'Aṭ-ṭābiq al-arḍī' = the ground floor.
Plural 'ḥadāʾiq'. 'Ḥadīqat al-ḥayawānāt' = zoo. Colloquial also 'junayna' (little paradise, from 'janna').
Plural 'shuqaq'. From sh-q-q (split), a part split off from a building. Colloquial Egyptian 'shaʾʾa'.
One step is a 'daraja', which is also 'degree' (temperature, grade). Same root as 'darrāja' (bicycle).
From 'thalj' (snow, ice). The faʿʿāla pattern names machines: ghassāla (washing machine), sayyāra (car).
Plural 'sajājīd'. From s-j-d (to prostrate), because of the prayer rug. 'Masjid' (mosque) is the same root.
Plural 'suṭūḥ'. Flat roofs are used for sleeping, washing and water tanks. Also 'surface' in geometry.
Also 'to be still'; 'sukūn' is the mark for 'no vowel'. 'Sākin' = resident (pl. sukkān, population). 'Maskan' = dwelling.
Root f-t-ḥ: 'miftāḥ' (key), 'fatḥa' (the a-vowel mark), 'al-Fātiḥa', 'Fatḥ' (the political movement). 'Maftūḥ' = open.
A form IV verb (afʿala). 'Mughlaq' = closed (on shop signs). Colloquial: 'sakkar' (Levant), 'ʾafal' (Egypt).
'Ṭabbākh' = cook (chef), 'maṭbakh' = kitchen, 'ṭabkha' = a dish. Colloquial also 'ṭabakh'.
'Ghassāla' = washing machine; 'ghusl' = the ritual full-body wash. 'Maghsala' = sink.
A form II verb (doubled middle letter), which often means 'to make X': from 'naẓīf' (clean). 'Tanẓīf' = cleaning.
Opposite 'wasikh' (dirty). 'Naẓāfa' = cleanliness; a proverb says 'an-naẓāfa min al-īmān' (cleanliness is part of faith).
A plural; the singular 'malbas' is rare. From l-b-s (to wear). Colloquial also 'hudūm' (Egypt), 'awāʿī' (Levant).
Plural 'qumṣān'. An ancient loan, related to Latin 'camisia', the source of 'chemise' and 'camisole'.
From French 'pantalon' (via Italian). Formal 'sirwāl', which is Persian in origin and gave Spanish 'zaragüelles'.
Plural 'fasātīn'. Borrowed from Turkish 'fistan', itself from Italian 'fustagno' (fustian cloth), a word once linked to Fustat (old Cairo).
Plural 'aḥdhiya'; one shoe or a pair. Colloquial 'gazma' (Egypt), 'ṣubbāṭ / kundara' (Levant). Shoes come off indoors.
Plural 'maʿāṭif'. From ʿ-ṭ-f (to wrap round, incline). Colloquial 'jākēt' for a jacket.
A Western-style hat; the traditional head covering of men in the Gulf and Levant is the 'ghutra' or 'kūfiyya' with a black cord ('ʿiqāl').
From ḥ-j-b (to veil, conceal). Also 'curtain, barrier' and an amulet. 'Muḥajjaba' = a woman who wears it.
Also the name of the whirling dervish dance in Egypt, from the dancer's wide skirt. Colloquial Egyptian 'jība / jūba' (from French 'jupe').
Plural of 'jawrab'. Colloquial 'sharāb' (Egypt), 'kalsāt' (Levant, from French 'chaussettes').
From Turkish 'çanta'. The formal word is 'ḥaqība'. Plural 'shunaṭ'. Colloquial Egyptian 'shanṭa', Levantine 'shante'.
From n-ẓ-r (look). 'Naẓẓārat shams' = sunglasses. Singular in form but means a pair.
Plural 'khawātim'. Originally a signet ring, from kh-t-m (to seal, finish): 'khātam an-nabiyyīn' = the seal of the prophets.
English 'cotton' comes from this word via Spanish 'algodón' (with the al- attached) and Old French. Egyptian cotton is famous.
'Ṭarīq al-ḥarīr' = the Silk Road. 'Ḥarīrī' = silky; also a family name (the Lebanese prime ministers).
From q-y-s (measure). 'Mā maqāsuk?' = what size are you? Also 'qiyās'.

example.en: Do you have a bigger size?

note: Root l-b-s: 'libās' (clothing), 'malābis'. Present 'yalbas'. Note the i-vowel in the past: 'labistu'.

example.en: I put on a heavy coat.

note: Also 'to depose' (a ruler) and 'to dislocate' (a joint). 'Khalaʿa ḥidhāʾahu' = he took off his shoes.
Plural 'judud'. 'Mā l-jadīd?' = what's new? 'Jaddada' = to renew; 'tajdīd' = renewal.
Plural 'qudamāʾ'. For people use 'kabīr fī s-sinn' or 'ʿajūz'. 'Al-Madīna l-Qadīma' = the old town.
'Ziyy rasmī' = uniform; 'ziyy' alone = costume, dress, as in 'az-ziyy al-waṭanī' (national dress). Plural 'azyāʾ' = fashions.
Plural 'juyūb'. In mathematics 'jayb' = sine: Latin 'sinus' is a translation of this very word (a famous mistranslation of a Sanskrit term).
Plural 'azrār'. Also a push button or key on a device: 'iḍghaṭ ʿalā z-zirr' = press the button.
Plural 'aḥzima'. 'Ḥizām al-amān' = seat belt. From ḥ-z-m (to tie up, be resolute: 'ḥazm').
'Anāqa' = elegance. Colloquial 'shīk' (from French) is equally common.
Plural 'waẓāʾif'. Also 'function' (of a device or in maths). 'Muwaẓẓaf' = employee, especially a civil servant.

example.en: I am looking for a job.

note: Past 'ʿamila', present 'yaʿmal'. Colloquial 'shtaghal / ishtaghal' (from 'shughl', work) is more common in speech.
Root d-r-s: 'dars' (lesson), 'madrasa' (school), 'mudarris' (teacher), 'dirāsa' (study). 'Darrasa' (form II) = to teach.

example.en: I studied Arabic for two years.

note: 'Qurʾān' is literally 'recitation', from this root; 'iqraʾ' (read!) was its first revealed word. 'Qāriʾ' = reader.
Form V (tafaʿʿala), reflexive of 'ʿallama' (teach). Root ʿ-l-m: 'ʿilm' (knowledge, science), 'ʿālim' (scholar), 'muʿallim' (teacher).
Form II of ʿ-l-m: to make someone know. 'Taʿlīm' = education; 'muʿallim' = teacher, also 'master craftsman' (Egypt: 'miʿallim').
Plural 'mudarrisūn'. 'Ustādh' (professor, also a polite 'sir') is a Persian loan used for teachers too.
Plural 'madāris'. The same letters as 'mudarrisa' (female teacher); vowels distinguish them. In English a 'madrasa' is specifically a religious college.
Plural 'jāmiʿāt'. Same root as 'jāmiʿ' (congregational mosque) and 'al-jumʿa' (Friday). Al-Azhar in Cairo is among the world's oldest.
Plural 'wājibāt'. From w-j-b (to be necessary). 'Al-wājib al-manzilī' = homework; also 'duty', as in 'lā shukra ʿalā wājib'.
Plural 'kutub'. Root k-t-b: 'kataba' (write), 'maktab' (office), 'maktaba' (library, bookshop), 'kātib' (writer). 'Al-Kitāb' = the Qurʾan.
Plural 'makātib'. 'Maktab al-barīd' = post office. 'Maktaba' with tāʾ marbūṭa is a library or bookshop.
Plural 'aqlām'. From Greek 'kalamos' (reed), since pens were cut reeds. 'Qalam raṣāṣ' (lead pen) = pencil.
'Waraq' = paper (collective), 'waraqa' = a sheet or a leaf; plural 'awrāq' (papers, documents). 'Waraq ʿinab' = stuffed vine leaves.
Plural 'lughāt'. 'Al-lugha l-ʿarabiyya' = the Arabic language. 'Lughawī' = linguistic.
Plural 'kalimāt'. From k-l-m (speak): 'kalām' (speech), 'takallama' (to talk). 'Kalimat as-sirr' = password.
Plural 'asʾila'. From 'saʾala' (to ask). The hamza sits on a wāw after a u-vowel, one of the hamza seat rules.
Plural 'ajwiba'. In Egypt 'gawāb' also means 'letter' (mail). 'Ajāba' = to answer; 'ijāba' = an answer.
Plural 'imtiḥānāt'. From m-ḥ-n (to test, afflict): 'miḥna' = ordeal. Colloquial 'imtiḥān' too.
From 'handasa' (geometry, engineering), a Persian loan ('andāza', measure). A respectful title: 'yā bāsh-muhandis' in Egypt.
Plural 'zumalāʾ'. Also 'classmate'. The faʿīl pattern with -āʾ plural is typical of people words (ṣadīq / aṣdiqāʾ).
Plural 'mudarāʾ'. From d-w-r (turn, run): the one who makes things run. 'Idāra' = administration.
Plural 'sharikāt'. From sh-r-k (share, be partner): 'sharīk' = partner. Colloquial 'shirka'.
Form VIII verbal noun of j-m-ʿ. 'ʿIlm al-ijtimāʿ' = sociology; 'ijtimāʿī' = social.
Coined from ḥ-s-b (count). In practice most people say 'kumbyūtar'; a laptop is 'lābtōb'.
'Kayfa ṭ-ṭaqs?' = how is the weather? 'Jaww' (air, atmosphere) is used the same way and also means 'mood'.
Feminine. The 'sun letters' (ḥurūf shamsiyya) are named after it: al- assimilates, so 'al-shams' is said 'ash-shams'. The moon is the opposite example.
Plural 'aqmār' (also 'satellites'). ق is a 'moon letter': al- stays 'al-qamar'. 'Qamar' is a common compliment for a beautiful face.
Plural 'amṭār'. 'Tumṭir' = it is raining. Colloquial Levantine 'shitā' means both winter and rain.
Plural 'riyāḥ'. Same root as 'rāʾiḥa' (smell) and 'rāḥa' (rest). Grammatically feminine.
One word for both snow and ice; 'thallāja' = fridge. 'Shāy bi-th-thalj' = iced tea. Plural 'thulūj'.
Collective; one cloud is 'saḥāba', plural 'suḥub'. 'Ghaym' is a synonym; 'ghāʾim' = cloudy.
'Al-jaww ḥārr' = it is hot. 'Ḥarr' = heat; 'ḥarāra' = temperature. For spicy food use 'ḥārr' too, or colloquial 'ḥāmī'.
'Bard' = the cold; 'bardān' = (I am) feeling cold. 'Māʾ bārid' = cold water. Colloquially 'bārid' can also mean 'boring'.

example.en: The weather is cold in winter.

note: 'Fī ṣ-ṣayf' = in summer. 'Maṣyaf' = summer resort. Seasons: rabīʿ, ṣayf, kharīf, shitāʾ.
In the Levant 'shitā' also means rain, since winter is the rainy season. 'Shatwī' = wintry.
'Ar-Rabīʿ al-ʿArabī' = the Arab Spring. Two Islamic months are called Rabīʿ al-Awwal and Rabīʿ ath-Thānī.
From kh-r-f (to pick fruit). In Dhofar (Oman) 'kharīf' is the monsoon season. 'Kharīfī' = autumnal.
Plural 'biḥār'. 'Al-Baḥr al-Abyaḍ al-Mutawassiṭ' = the Mediterranean. 'Baḥrayn' (Bahrain) is the dual: two seas.
Plural 'jibāl'. Gibraltar is 'Jabal Ṭāriq' (Ṭāriq's mountain), after the commander who crossed in 711.
Plural 'anhār'. 'Nahr an-Nīl' = the Nile; 'nahr al-Urdunn' = the Jordan. Same letters as 'nahār' (daytime).
English 'Sahara' is simply this word. Feminine (the faʿlāʾ pattern); plural 'ṣaḥārā'.
'Shajar' (collective) / 'shajara' (one tree), plural 'ashjār'. 'Shajarat al-ʿāʾila' = family tree.
'Zahr' collective, 'zahra' one flower, plural 'zuhūr' or 'azhār'. Al-Azhar (the most radiant) is named with the same root.
Feminine; plural 'samāwāt' (heavens). 'Samāwī' = sky-blue. Root s-m-w, 'to be high'.
Plural 'ḥayawānāt'. From ḥ-y-y (to live): 'ḥayāt' = life. 'Ḥadīqat al-ḥayawānāt' = zoo.
'Qiṭṭ' (m.) / 'qiṭṭa' (f.), plural 'qiṭaṭ'. Colloquial 'biss / bissa' (Levant), 'ʾuṭṭa' (Egypt). Related to Latin 'cattus'.
Plural 'kilāb'; feminine 'kalba'. Calling someone 'kalb' is a serious insult. Colloquial Egyptian pronounces it 'kalb' too, unlike many q/g shifts.
Plural 'jimāl'. English 'camel' (via Greek 'kamēlos') is a Semitic loan. The letter name 'gimel/gamma' is said to come from this word.
From 'shams'. 'Yawm mushmis' = a sunny day. 'Mumṭir' = rainy, 'ghāʾim' = cloudy.
Plural 'aswāq'. English 'souk' is this word. Turkish 'çarşı' and Persian 'bāzār' are the other regional words.
Plural 'maḥallāt'. Also 'dukkān' (small shop, pl. dakākīn) and 'matjar' (store). 'Maḥallī' = local.
Plural of 'naqd' (cash, coin). Colloquial: 'fulūs' (originally 'coppers', pl. of fals), 'maṣārī' (Levant).
Plural 'asʿār'. 'Bi-kam?' or 'mā s-siʿr?' = how much? 'Siʿr aṣ-ṣarf' = exchange rate.
'Bi-' (for, with) + 'kam' (how much). Answer: 'bi-ʿashara' = ten. Colloquial Egyptian 'bi-kām'.
A defective adjective: 'ghālin' alone, 'al-ghālī' with al-, feminine 'ghāliya'. Colloquial 'ghālī'. Also 'dear, precious' of people.
'Arkhaṣ' = cheaper. 'Rukhṣa' from the same root means a licence or permit.
Form VIII of sh-r-y. Weak final: 'ishtaraytu' (I bought). 'Mushtarī' = buyer, and the planet Jupiter.
Hollow verb: 'bāʿa' but 'biʿtu' (I sold). 'Bāʾiʿ' = seller; 'bayʿ' = sale; 'mabīʿāt' = sales.
Also 'to push' (on doors: 'idfaʿ' = push, 'isḥab' = pull). 'Dafʿ' = payment; 'madfūʿ' = paid.
Form II. 'Kam yukallif?' = how much does it cost? 'Taklifa' = cost; 'takālīf' = expenses. Colloquial 'bi-kam' is more usual than any verb.
From ṣ-r-f (to change money, spend). 'Bank' is used just as often; 'Maṣrif Lubnān' is Lebanon's central bank.
'Biṭāqat iʾtimān' = credit card; 'biṭāqa shakhṣiyya' = ID card. Colloquial also 'kart'.
The adverbial -an form of 'naqd'. 'Naqd' also means 'criticism' (literary or film).
Also 'opponent' in a dispute. 'Takhfīḍ' (reduction) and 'tanzīlāt' (sales) appear on shop windows.
From w-ṣ-l (reach, deliver). Also 'waṣl' or colloquial 'fātūra' (invoice, from Italian 'fattura').
Plural 'hadāyā'. From h-d-y (guide, lead); 'ahdā' = to give as a gift.
Currency of Jordan, Iraq, Kuwait, Bahrain, Algeria, Tunisia and Libya. From Latin 'denarius'. Plural 'danānīr'.
Egyptian and Sudanese pound; from English 'guinea'. Syria and Lebanon use the 'līra', Saudi Arabia the 'riyāl', the UAE the 'dirham'.
'Majjānī' = free (adjective). Not the same as 'ḥurr' (free, at liberty).
Form III. Haggling is expected in souks, not in supermarkets. Colloquial Egyptian 'fāṣil', Levantine 'fāṣal'.
Short for 'kīlūghrām'. 'Kīlū ṭamāṭim' = a kilo of tomatoes. Fruit and vegetables are priced per kilo in markets.
'Kathīran' = a lot, often (adverb). 'Akthar' = more, most. Colloquial 'ktīr' (Levant), 'kitīr' (Egypt).
'Qalīlan' = a little (adverb). 'Qalīl min' = a bit of. Colloquial 'shwayya' is the everyday word for 'a little'.
A plain loanword. The official coinage 'matjar kabīr' is rarely heard. Prices there are fixed, unlike in the sūq.
Plural 'suʿadāʾ'. 'Saʿāda' = happiness, also the title 'Excellency'. Port Said (Būr Saʿīd) is named after a khedive. Colloquial 'mabsūṭ'.

example.en: I am happy to meet you.

note: 'Ḥuzn' = sadness, grief. The faʿīl pattern gives many such adjectives (saʿīd, kabīr). Colloquial 'zaʿlān' covers both sad and upset.
'Ghaḍab' = anger. Colloquial: 'zaʿlān' (Levant/Egypt, also 'upset'), 'miʿaṣṣab' (nervy).
Active participle of 'khāfa'. 'Khawf' = fear. Colloquial 'khāyif / khāyfa'. 'Lā takhaf' = don't be afraid.
A doubled form IV verb: 'aḥabba' but 'aḥbabtu' (I loved). Present 'uḥibb'. 'Ḥubb' = love; 'ḥabīb / ḥabībī' = darling.
'Karāhiya' = hatred; 'makrūh' = disliked, a category in Islamic law. Present 'yakrah'.
Hollow verb: 'khāfa' but 'khiftu' (I was afraid). 'Khāfa min' = to be afraid of. 'Makhūf' = dreaded.

example.en: I was afraid of the dog.

note: 'Ḍaḥik' = laughter; 'muḍḥik' = funny. ض, the 'ḍād', is so distinctive that Arabic is called 'lughat aḍ-ḍād'.
Weak final: 'bakaytu' (I cried). 'Bukāʾ' = crying. 'Ḥāʾiṭ al-mabkā' = the Wailing Wall.
'Faraḥ' = joy, and also 'wedding' in Egypt. 'Farḥān' = glad. 'Fariḥa bi-' = to be happy about.

example.en: I was glad at the news.

note: 'Ḥubbī' = my love. 'Ḥabba' with a tāʾ marbūṭa means 'a grain, a pill'. Root ḥ-b-b.
'Lā khawf' = no fear, no worries. The hollow root kh-w-f shows its wāw here but not in 'khāfa'.
From 'mufājaʾa' (surprise). Colloquial also 'mitfāji' / 'mistaghrib' (finding it strange).
'Malal' = boredom; 'mumill' = boring. Colloquial 'zahqān' (Egypt), 'malān' (Levant).
'Qalaq' = worry, anxiety. 'Lā taqlaq' = don't worry. Colloquial 'ʾalqān' (Egypt).
'Hudūʾ' = calm, quiet. 'Al-Muḥīṭ al-Hādiʾ' = the Pacific Ocean. 'Ihdaʾ!' = calm down.
'Fakhūr bi-' = proud of. 'Fakhr' = pride (positive); 'kibr' is arrogance. Fakhr ad-Dīn is a name ('pride of the faith').
'Khajal' = shyness, embarrassment. Colloquial 'maksūf' (embarrassed), from 'kasafa' (to eclipse, to shame).
From r-w-ḥ (rest): 'rāḥa' = rest, comfort; 'istarāḥa' = to rest. 'Anā murtāḥ hunā' = I feel at ease here.
Also 'only': 'ibnī l-waḥīd' = my only son. From w-ḥ-d (one): 'wāḥid', 'tawḥīd' (monotheism). 'Waḥda' = loneliness, and unity.
Plural 'āmāl'. 'Amal' is a popular girl's name. 'Ātamal an' = I hope that. Not 'alam' (pain), which has the same letters.
'Ishtāqa ilā' = to miss someone. Hollow form VIII: 'ishtaqtu ilayk' = I missed you. 'Shawq' = longing. Colloquial 'waḥashtanī' (Egypt).
Form VIII. 'Ibtisāma' = a smile. 'Ibtasim!' = smile! Colloquial Egyptian 'ibtasam'.
'Rāʾiʿ!' is the everyday exclamation for 'awesome'. From r-w-ʿ, originally 'startling'. 'Rawāʾiʿ' = masterpieces.
'Nuʿās' = drowsiness. Another faʿlān state adjective (ʿaṭshān, taʿbān, zaʿlān). Formal feminine 'naʿsā'.
Present 'yaʾkul', imperative 'kul'. 'Akl' = food (colloquial). 'Mākūlāt' = foods, dishes.
Present 'yashrab'. 'Sharāb' = drink, syrup; 'mashrūb' = beverage. English 'sherbet', 'sorbet' and 'syrup' all go back to this root.
Hollow: 'qāla' but 'qultu' (I said). Present 'yaqūl'. 'Qawl' = saying; 'maqāl' = article. Colloquial 'ʾāl' (Egypt), 'ʾāl / gāl' (Gulf).
Hollow with final hamza: 'jiʾtu' (I came). Present 'yajīʾ'. Colloquial 'ijā' (Levant), 'gih' (Egypt); 'taʿāl' = come!
Weak final with hamza: 'raʾaytu' (I saw). The present 'yarā' drops the hamza entirely. 'Raʾy' = opinion; 'ruʾya' = vision.
Form IV, weak final: 'aʿṭaytu' (I gave). Imperative 'aʿṭinī' = give me. 'ʿAṭāʾ' = giving, generosity.
Present 'yaʾkhudh', imperative 'khudh'. 'Maʾkhadh' = source, outlet; 'muʾākhadha' = reproach ('lā muʾākhadha' = no offence).
Hollow form IV: 'aradtu' (I wanted); present 'urīd'. 'Irāda' = will. In speech people use 'biddī', 'ʿāyiz', 'abghā' instead.
Hollow form X: 'istaṭaʿtu' (I could); present 'astaṭīʿ'. Colloquial: 'ʾidir' (Egypt), 'ʾidir / fī' (Levant).
Form V from k-l-m. 'Atakallam al-ʿarabiyya' = I speak Arabic. Colloquial 'ḥakā' (Levant), 'itkallim' (Egypt).
Form X of y-q-ẓ. Colloquial 'ṣiḥī' (Egypt), 'fāʾ' (Levant). 'Yaqẓa' = wakefulness, vigilance.
'Maʿrifa' = knowledge (of a person or thing); 'ʿalima' is knowing a fact. 'Lā aʿrif' = I don't know. 'ʿArafāt' is the plain near Mecca.
Present 'yafham'. 'Fāhim?' = got it? 'Mafhūm' = understood, and 'concept'. Colloquial 'fihim'.
Present 'yasmaʿ'. 'Samīʿ' (all-hearing) is a name of God; 'Ismāʿīl' (Ishmael) means 'God hears'. 'Istamaʿa ilā' = to listen to.
Form III. 'Shāhid' = witness; 'mushāhid' = viewer; 'shahāda' = testimony, certificate and the profession of faith.
Form III. 'Musāʿada' = help; 'sāʿidnī' = help me! From 'sāʿid' (forearm): to lend an arm.
Present 'yadkhul'. 'Madkhal' = entrance; 'dākhil' = inside; 'dakhl' = income. 'Udkhul' = come in.
Present 'yakhruj'. 'Makhraj' = exit; 'khārij' = outside, abroad; 'khurūj' = Exodus (the book).
Present 'yajlis', imperative 'ijlis'. 'Majlis' = council, sitting room (as in Majlis ash-Shūrā). Colloquial 'ʾaʿad'.
Present 'yaqif' (the w drops), imperative 'qif' (stop sign). 'Mawqif' = stop, position; 'waqf' = a religious endowment.
Not needed in present-tense sentences, but required for the past: 'kāna ṭabīban' = he was a doctor. Hollow: 'kuntu' (I was). 'Makān' = place.
The model root grammarians use for all patterns: faʿala, fāʿil, mafʿūl. 'Fiʿl' = verb, deed. In speech 'ʿamal' or 'sawwā' are more usual.
Present 'yalʿab'. 'Luʿba' = game, toy; 'lāʿib' = player; 'malʿab' = playground, stadium.
Also 'to be pregnant' ('ḥāmil'). 'Ḥammāl' = porter; 'maḥmūl' = mobile phone (the carried one); 'ḥamla' = campaign.
Hollow: 'ʿudtu' (I returned); present 'yaʿūd'. 'ʿĪd' (festival) is the same root: the day that comes back. 'ʿĀda' = habit, custom.
Used before verbs: 'mādhā turīd?' (what do you want?). Before nouns use 'mā': 'mā hādhā?' (what is this?). Colloquial 'ē' (Egypt), 'shū' (Levant).
Spelled like 'min' (from); the fatḥa here shows the difference. 'Man hādhā?' = who is this? Colloquial 'mīn'.
Colloquial 'ēmta' (Egypt), 'ēmta / waqtēsh' (Levant), 'mitā' (Gulf). Ends in alif maqṣūra.
'Li-' (for) + 'mādhā' (what). Colloquial 'lē' (Egypt), 'lēsh' (Levant/Gulf).
'Kayfa l-ḥāl?' = how are you? Colloquial 'izzāy' (Egypt), 'kīf' (Levant), 'shlōn' (Iraq/Gulf, 'what colour').
Followed by a singular noun: 'kam kitāban?' (how many books?). 'Bi-kam' = how much (price); 'kam as-sāʿa' = what time.
Starts a yes/no question with no English equivalent: 'hal anta ṭālib?' = are you a student? Colloquial speech drops it and uses intonation.
'Ayy kitāb?' = which book? Feminine 'ayya'. Also 'any': 'ayy shayʾ' = anything.
The final alif is silent: pronounced 'ana' with a short vowel. No gender form needed.
'Anta' to a man, 'anti' to a woman: identical without vowel marks. Plural 'antum' (m.), 'antunna' (f.). Colloquial 'inta / inti'.
Also 'it' for masculine nouns, since every noun has a gender. Colloquial 'huwwa' (Egypt), 'huwwe' (Levant).
Also 'it' for feminine nouns, and used for non-human plurals ('al-kutub, hiya...'). Colloquial 'hiyya / hiyye'.
Colloquial 'iḥna' (Egypt/Gulf), 'niḥna' (Levant). The verb ending for 'we' is '-nā': 'dhahabnā' = we went.
Masculine or mixed group; 'hunna' for an all-female group, 'humā' for two. Colloquial 'humma' (Egypt), 'hinne' (Levant).
'Hādhā' (m.) / 'hādhihi' (f.). The long ā after h is not written: a 'dagger alif' in vowelled texts. 'Dhālika' = that.
'Fī l-bayt' = at home. Colloquially also 'there is': 'fī mushkila' = there's a problem; 'mā fī' = there isn't.
Ends in alif maqṣūra, which becomes 'ay' before suffixes: 'ʿalayk' (on you), as in 'as-salāmu ʿalaykum'.
'Maʿī' = with me; 'maʿa s-salāma' = (go) with safety. Also 'to have on one': 'maʿak fulūs?' = have you got money on you?
'Anā min...' = I am from... Also 'than' in comparisons: 'akbar min' = bigger than. Same letters as 'man' (who).
'Ilā l-liqāʾ' = until the meeting. Becomes 'ilay-' before suffixes: 'ilayk' (to you). Colloquial 'la-' or 'ʿalā'.
Always attached to the next word with no space: 'anā wa-anta' is written أنا وأنت. Arabic strings many clauses with 'wa'.
The long ā is not written (dagger alif). 'Lākinna' before a noun or pronoun suffix: 'lākinnī' = but I. Colloquial 'bass'.
'Shāy aw qahwa?' = tea or coffee? In questions offering a choice, 'am' is the classical form.
'Li-' + 'anna' (that). Followed by a noun or pronoun suffix: 'li-annī' = because I. Colloquial 'ʿashān' (Egypt), 'laʾinnu' (Levant).
Comes after the adjective: 'kabīr jiddan' = very big. Colloquial 'ʾawī' (Egypt), 'ktīr' (Levant), 'wāyid' (Gulf).
'Jamāl' = beauty (also a name, as in Gamal Abdel Nasser). 'Jamal' (camel) has the same consonants. Colloquial 'ḥilw' is often used instead.
One word for both tall and long. Plural 'ṭiwāl'. 'Ṭūl' = length, height; 'ʿalā ṭūl' = straight ahead.
Plural 'qiṣār'. 'Qiṣṣa qaṣīra' = short story. 'Qaṣṣara' = to shorten.
'Jayyid jiddan' = very good (on school work). Colloquial: 'kwayyis' (Egypt), 'mnīḥ' (Levant), 'zēn' (Gulf/Iraq).
The hamza sits on a yāʾ-shaped seat after a kasra. Colloquial 'wiḥish' (Egypt), 'ʿāṭil' (Levant). 'Sayyiʾa' = a bad deed, sin.
Also 'plain, lowland' as a noun, as in 'ahlan wa-sahlan'. 'Bi-suhūla' = easily.
'Ṣuʿūba' = difficulty. Colloquial 'ṣaʿb' everywhere. 'Aṣʿab' = harder.
Sweet to taste, and colloquially 'nice, pretty, cool'. 'Ḥalawiyyāt' = sweets. 'Al-ḥulwa' = the pretty one.
'Māʾ sākhin' = hot water; 'mashrūbāt sākhina' = hot drinks. For weather use 'ḥārr'. 'Sakhkhān' = water heater.
'Quwwa' = strength, power (as in 'al-quwwāt', armed forces). Colloquial Egyptian 'ʾawī' means 'very'.
Plural 'ḍuʿafāʾ'. 'Ḍaʿf' = weakness. In hadith studies a 'ḍaʿīf' report is one with a weak chain of transmission.
Plural 'aghniyāʾ'. 'Ghinā' = wealth; 'ghināʾ' (with hamza) = singing, a different root. 'Al-Ghanī' is a name of God.
Plural 'fuqarāʾ'. English 'fakir' is this word: a religious mendicant. 'Faqr' = poverty.
Plural 'adhkiyāʾ'. 'Dhakāʾ' = intelligence; 'adh-dhakāʾ al-iṣṭināʿī' = artificial intelligence. 'Hātif dhakī' = smartphone.
Passive participle of 'shahara' (make known). 'Shuhra' = fame. Same root as 'shahr' (month, from the new moon being 'announced').
'Muhimma' = a task or mission. 'Lā yuhimm' = it doesn't matter. 'Ahamm' = more important.
Both 'strange' and 'stranger / foreigner'; plural 'ghurabāʾ'. From gh-r-b (west, setting sun): 'ghurba' = living abroad.
'Al-Laṭīf' is a name of God (the Subtle, Kind). 'Laṭīfa' is a common woman's name. 'Luṭf' = kindness, grace.
Passive participle of 'shaghala' (occupy). 'Shughl' = work (colloquial). 'Al-khaṭṭ mashghūl' = the line is busy.
'Jāhiz?' = ready? 'Malābis jāhiza' = ready-made clothes. 'Jahhaza' = to prepare, equip; 'jihāz' = device.
Also 'tiresome' of a person ('thaqīl ad-dam', heavy-blooded). 'Thiql' = weight.
'Khafīf ad-dam' (light of blood) = charming, funny. 'Wajba khafīfa' = a light meal, snack.
Opposite ḍayyiq (narrow). From w-s-ʿ: wusʿ = capacity, tawassuʿ = expansion. Al-Wāsiʿ (the All-Embracing) is a name of God.
From kh-l-f (differ, come after): 'ikhtilāf' = difference, 'khalīfa' = successor (caliph). 'Mukhtalif ʿan' = different from.
The top grade in school and the premium petrol pump. From m-y-z (distinguish): 'imtiyāz' = privilege, distinction.
Plural 'mudun'. Al-Madīna (Medina) is 'the city' par excellence. 'Madanī' = civil, urban; 'tamaddun' = civilisation.
Plural 'quran'. 'Umm al-Qurā' (mother of villages) is a traditional name of Mecca. Colloquial Levantine 'ḍayʿa'.
Plural 'bilād' (which is also 'country' as in 'Bilād ash-Shām'), or 'buldān'. 'Baladī' = local, of the home town.
Plural 'masājid'. From s-j-d (to prostrate). English 'mosque' came via Spanish 'mezquita'. 'Jāmiʿ' is the big Friday mosque.
Plural 'kanāʾis'. From Aramaic/Syriac 'knishta' (assembly), related to Hebrew 'knesset'.
Plural 'maktabāt'. Both a library and a bookshop or stationer's; context decides. Root k-t-b.
Plural 'matāḥif'. From 'tuḥfa' (masterpiece, precious object). 'Al-Matḥaf al-Miṣrī' = the Egyptian Museum.
Plural 'mayādīn'. 'Maydān at-Taḥrīr' = Tahrir Square. Also 'field' (of study, of battle). Levantine 'sāḥa'.
'Shurṭī' = policeman; 'markaz ash-shurṭa' = police station. Colloquial 'būlīs' (from 'police') is also common.
'Barīd' (post) originally meant the relay courier of the caliphs. 'Barīd iliktrūnī' = e-mail.
Plural 'mabānī'. From b-n-y (build): 'bināʾ' = construction, 'bannāʾ' = builder. Colloquial 'ʿimāra' = apartment block.
Plural 'ʿawāṣim'. From ʿ-ṣ-m (protect). 'ʿĀṣimat Miṣr al-Qāhira' = Egypt's capital is Cairo.
Plural 'aḥyāʾ'. Also the adjective 'alive'. 'Al-Ḥayy al-Qadīm' = the old quarter. Colloquial Egyptian 'ḥitta' or 'manṭiʾa'.
Plural 'abrāj' (also the signs of the zodiac). 'Burj Khalīfa' in Dubai. Related to Greek 'pyrgos' and German 'Burg'.
Plural 'qilāʿ'. 'Qalʿat Ṣalāḥ ad-Dīn' is Cairo's citadel. Spanish 'Alcalá' and many place names come from 'al-qalʿa'.
A loanword. Egypt's film industry made Egyptian Arabic understood across the whole region.
Plural 'shawāṭiʾ'. The hamza sits on a yāʾ seat after a kasra. 'Sāḥil' = coast (as in the Sahel, the 'shore' of the Sahara).
Plural 'marākiz'. 'Markaz al-madīna' = city centre; 'markaz tijārī' = shopping mall. 'Markazī' = central.
'Safīr' = ambassador (pl. sufarāʾ). From s-f-r, the root of 'safar' (travel) and 'sāfara'.
Plural 'ʿanāwīn'. Also 'title' of a book or article. 'Mā ʿunwānuk?' = what is your address?
Weak final: 'mashaytu' (I walked). 'Mashyan' = on foot. In colloquial 'māshī' means 'OK, fine' (literally 'walking').

example.en: We walked in the old town.

note: Hollow: 'zurtu' (I visited). 'Ziyāra' = visit; 'zāʾir' = visitor; 'mazār' = shrine. 'Zūrūnā' = visit us!
Present 'yajid' (the w drops). 'Mawjūd' = present, available: 'mish mawjūd' = not here. 'Wujūd' = existence.
From z-ḥ-m (to crowd). The everyday word for crowds and traffic in Cairo and Beirut. 'Izdiḥām' is the formal term.
Plural 'quṣūr'. From Latin 'castrum' (fort), via Aramaic. Spanish 'alcázar' = 'al-qaṣr'. Luxor is 'al-Uqṣur', 'the palaces'.
